kzz7yh-a78920-d1e103.summary: Announces four questions on the second principal topic of the distinction, the existence of an angel in place.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e112.summary: First question: whether an angel is nowhere.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e114.summary: Second question: whether an angel is in an extended space or in some indivisible part of space such as a point.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e121.summary: Third question: whether an angel can be in several places at once.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e127.summary: Fourth question: whether several angels can be in the same place at once.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e136.summary: Beginning of the first argument that an angel is nowhere, from Boethius's De hebdomadibus (continued in the next paragraph).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e143.summary: Completion of the Boethian argument: it is a common conception, approved by the learned, that incorporeals are not in place; an angel is incorporeal, so it is not in place and therefore nowhere.
claims: Incorporeal things are not in place (objection).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e152.summary: Second argument: Augustine (83 Questions) says what is somewhere is contained by place and what is contained by place is a body; an angel is not a body, so it is nowhere.
claims: Only bodies are contained in place (objection).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e161.summary: Third argument: Avicenna says intelligible substances have no position and cannot be pointed to.
claims: Intelligible substances lack situs (objection).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e171.summary: Fourth argument: Avicenna says what is not sensible has no place at all; an angel is not sensible.
claims: Non-sensible things have no place (objection).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e178.summary: Fifth argument: the outermost heaven is nowhere (Physics IV), and it is more reasonable for an angel to be nowhere than any corporeal substance.
claims: The outermost heaven is nowhere (objection).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e187.summary: Sixth argument: being nowhere is not repugnant to angelic nature, since if the corporeal world were destroyed the angel would remain and be nowhere; so likewise now.
claims: Angelic nature is compatible with being nowhere (objection).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e196.summary: Seventh argument: God could create another world, move the angels there and then destroy it without changing them, leaving them nowhere while this world remains; so the world's existence does not force angels to be somewhere.
claims: God could make angels be nowhere while this world remains (objection).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e220.summary: Eighth argument: if angels are in place whenever place exists, then if only a millet seed existed, all angels would be in it, which is absurd.
claims: Angels' location cannot follow merely from the existence of place (objection).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e227.summary: Sed contra from John of Damascus: heaven contains visible and invisible creatures, angels included.
claims: Angels are contained within heaven.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e237.summary: Second sed contra: Aristotle (De caelo I) reports that all peoples agree that the first heaven is the place of spiritual beings; angels are spiritual, so they are in heaven.
claims: Common consent places spiritual beings in the highest heaven.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e248.summary: Third sed contra: Aristotle says spiritual things are in the upper heaven, the world's horizon.
claims: Spiritual things are in the upper heaven.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e257.summary: Fourth sed contra from Cicero (Tusculans I): whatever exists must be somewhere; angels exist, so they cannot be nowhere.
claims: Whatever exists must be somewhere.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e268.summary: Fifth sed contra: Physics IV, what is not is nowhere and what is is somewhere; angels exist, so they are somewhere.
claims: What exists is somewhere.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e275.summary: Sixth sed contra: since being precedes operating by order of nature, being in place precedes operating in place.
claims: Being in place is naturally prior to operating in place.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e280.summary: Reports an opinion that an angel without an assumed body is in place only by operation: things are applied to place by commensuration (bodies), by informing a located body (soul), or as boundary of a positioned thing (point); since none fits an angel, only operation remains.
claims: An angel is in place only by operation (reported opinion).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e307.summary: Against that opinion, authority: Walafrid Strabo's gloss on Genesis 1 says the empyrean heaven was at once filled with angels, which cannot mean by operation.
claims: Angels filled the empyrean at creation independently of any operation.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e320.summary: Further authority: Hugh of St Victor (De sacramentis I.3.13) rejects those who remove place from every spirit because they define place only by corporeal dimension.
claims: Denying spirits all place departs from common judgment.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e336.summary: Notes that those teaching the opinion were excommunicated by Stephen, Bishop of Paris (the 1277 Condemnation).
claims: The operation-only theory of angelic location was condemned at Paris.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e341.summary: Adds that the authorities cited earlier in the sed contra also oppose that opinion.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e348.summary: Richard's argument and solution: angels move bodies such as the orbs, and the mover's power must be applied to the mobile before motion begins; so the angel is present to a body before any operation in it. Hence an angel is in place independently of operation, not circumscriptively but definitively. The efficient reason of this application is the angel's will and power, or God's; its final reason is the unity of the universe or intended operation. Its formal reason is none of circumscription, information, termination or operation but the angel's 'simultas', its togetherness with the place or with the thing in place, as circumscription is the formal reason for bodies.
claims: An angel is present to a body by nature prior to operating in it.
An angel is in place definitively, not circumscriptively.
The formal reason of an angel's being in place is its simultas with the place.
The efficient cause of the application is the angel's will and power or God's power; its final cause is the order of the universe.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e431.summary: This answers the rival opinion's reason: its division of ways of being in place was insufficient.
claims: The rival opinion's enumeration of modes of location is incomplete.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e437.summary: Transition to replies to the arguments that an angel is nowhere.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e442.summary: Reply to Boethius: he denies only that incorporeals are in place circumscriptively, not that they are present by simultas with place; the next three arguments are solved likewise.
claims: Authorities denying spirits are in place mean only circumscriptive place.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e453.summary: Reply to the fifth argument: the outermost heaven, though not contained by a place, is applied to the thing in place by active circumscription.
claims: The outermost heaven is located by actively containing, not being contained.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e460.summary: Reply to the sixth argument, first view: some say an angel cannot be nowhere while the world remains, because coming from one principle the angel must be applied to some part of the world, though no determinate part.
claims: Given the world, an angel must be applied to some part of it (reported view).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e480.summary: Second view, which Richard endorses ('ita dico'): as being nowhere is not repugnant to angelic nature, neither is being somewhere; it would be nowhere without a corporeal world, but given the world it is somewhere.
claims: An angel is somewhere given the corporeal world, though it could be nowhere without one.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e491.summary: Reply to the seventh argument: it shows only that God could make angels not in place while the world remains, which some grant, since angelic location belongs to the accidental order of the universe, not its essential order (the graded participation of the first being), and God can alter the former while keeping the latter. The question, however, concerns what is, not what God could do.
claims: Angelic location belongs to the accidental, not essential, order of the universe.
God could alter the accidental order while preserving the essential order.
concepts: essential vs accidental order of the universe

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e510.summary: Reply to the eighth argument: angels' being in place follows not from the existence of any place whatsoever but from the world as presently ordered; with only a millet seed left, angels need not be in it, lacking the same relation to it.
claims: Angelic location follows from the ordered world, not from place as such.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e528.summary: The sed contra arguments are conceded for their conclusion, but the last is formally invalid: by parity one could argue that being in time precedes moving in time, which fails since a thing is in time through its motion (Physics IV).
claims: The argument from priority of being over operation is formally invalid.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e544.summary: First argument that an angel is not in extended space: as things in an indivisible place are indivisible (De anima I), so indivisible things lack divisible place; an angel is indivisible and all space divisible.
claims: Indivisibles cannot occupy divisible space (objection).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e562.summary: Second argument: as a divisible body cannot be in an indivisible, so an indivisible angel cannot be in a divisible.
claims: Indivisible and divisible cannot be located in each other (objection).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e569.summary: Third argument: an indivisible angel would more plausibly be in a point than in space; but it cannot be in a point, since not even the soul is in a point of its body, so much less in space.
claims: An angel cannot be in a point (objection).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e578.summary: Fourth argument: what is in space is in place imaginably, but John of Damascus says an angel is in place intelligibly.
claims: Angels are in place intelligibly, not imaginably (objection).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e588.summary: Sed contra: per Damascene, an angel is where it operates, and it operates immediately in each part of a space; so it is in a whole space.
claims: An angel is where it operates.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e597.summary: Second sed contra: the soul, less simple than an angel, is whole in each part of its body as form; a fortiori a simpler angel can be in a body so as to be whole in every part, though not as form.
claims: Simplicity allows a spirit to be whole in every part of a space.
concepts: totus in toto et in qualibet parte

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e608.summary: Richard's solution: an angel is in corporeal space, and the space to which it can be present at once has a maximum but no minimum limit. Being undimensioned, it is not present part to part, neither commensurated nor circumscribed, but whole to the whole space and whole in each part.
claims: An angel is present in extended space, whole in the whole and whole in each part.
The space an angel can occupy has an upper limit but no lower limit.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e628.summary: Explains by distinguishing four simplicities: negative simplicity of magnitude (a point, neither extended nor apt to be), privative simplicity (bodily substance separated by God from its dimensions, apt but not extended), positive simplicity of spiritual immensity (God, whose simplicity grounds his immensity), and positive simplicity of a finite spiritual magnitude falling infinitely short of immensity (created spirits like souls and angels).
claims: There are four kinds of simplicity: negative, privative, positive-immense and positive-finite.
Divine simplicity is the reason of divine immensity.
Created spirits have a positive but finite spiritual magnitude.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e657.summary: Because an angel's simplicity is a positive, finite spiritual magnitude, a remote and weak imitation of divine immensity, it can be present to a whole space at once and, by its simplicity, be in every part of it.
claims: Angelic presence in space imitates divine immensity in a limited way.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e677.summary: Reply to the first and second arguments: a divisible cannot be in an indivisible, but it does not follow that an indivisible cannot be in a divisible, since spiritual indivisibility includes positive spiritual magnitude.
claims: Spiritual indivisibles can be in divisible space.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e696.summary: Reply to the third argument: it proves too much, since then the angel would be nowhere. Some say an angel is not in a point, since a point is not a place, and deny that an indivisible with spiritual magnitude is more plausibly in a point.
claims: The objection proves too much.
A point is not a place (one view).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e714.summary: Others say an angel can be in a point by its simplicity, since an angel need not follow the laws of place and a point is not supremely simple. The soul is unlike, being in the body as form, whereas a point is not a body or part of one; a separated soul could be in every indivisible of its place.
claims: An angel can be in a point (alternative view).
The soul's relation to its body as form differs from location.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e736.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: Damascene's 'intelligibly' means not circumscriptively; though the space is imaginable, the angel and its mode of being there are grasped by reason, not imagination.
claims: Angels' mode of location is grasped by reason, not imagination.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e752.summary: First argument for angelic multilocation: Hugh of St Victor says God can make one body be locally in diverse places, so likewise an angel.
claims: God can make a body be in several places (argument).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e765.summary: Second argument: Richard of St Victor says in two wise persons there is one wisdom; likewise one angel can be in two places.
claims: One wisdom in two wise persons (argument).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e772.summary: Third argument: the legend of St Martin reports that Ambrose, asleep at the altar in Milan, attended Martin's funeral; so one can be in two places, a fortiori an angel.
claims: Ambrose was in two places at once (argument from legend).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e788.summary: Fourth argument: Augustine (City of God 18) tells of a sleeping person's 'phantasticum' appearing to others in animal form, implying presence in two places; an angel is less limited.
claims: A sleeper's phantasticum can appear elsewhere (argument).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e802.summary: Fifth argument: water and air are two places, yet an angel can be in part of each at once if together they do not exceed its maximum space.
claims: An angel can span two bodies' places (argument).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e813.summary: Sed contra from Damascene: angels in heaven are not on earth, and when sent to earth do not remain in heaven.
claims: Angels do not remain in heaven when sent to earth.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e824.summary: Second sed contra from Damascene: an angel cannot operate in diverse places at once, but it can operate wherever it is.
claims: An angel cannot operate in several places at once.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e831.summary: Richard's solution: one angel cannot be in diverse places at once by any created power. Otherwise its space would have no maximum, since if it could be in two places a league apart, it could be in places at any distance, which exceeds being in one place however large. Being definitively in place means being defined by one's place, which would fail if one could also be elsewhere; this is so evident as to be nearly per se notum, and it seems to imply a contradiction.
claims: No created power can make an angel be in several places at once.
Definitive location excludes simultaneous presence elsewhere.
Angelic multilocation by its own power implies contradiction.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e875.summary: Reply to Hugh: this shows only what God could do supernaturally, whereas the question concerns what the angel can do by its own power.
claims: Supernatural divine power is outside the question.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e888.summary: Reply to Richard of St Victor: the text must be expounded of uncreated wisdom, which, being unlimited, can be in many.
claims: Only unlimited wisdom can be in many at once.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e898.summary: Reply to the Ambrose legend: either it happened supernaturally by divine power, or neither Ambrose's body nor soul was present but an angel appeared in his likeness while he dreamt he was attending.
claims: Ambrose's bilocation was either miraculous or an angelic apparition.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e914.summary: Reply to Augustine's phantasticum: nothing really leaves the sleeper; the sleeper dreams of being present while some spirit appears in his likeness to the observer.
claims: The phantasticum does not leave the sleeper; a spirit counterfeits his appearance.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e930.summary: Reply to the fifth argument: parts of air and water together not exceeding the angel's maximum space count as one place for the angel.
claims: Contiguous parts within the angel's maximum space constitute one angelic place.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e946.summary: First argument that several angels can be in one place: a glorified body can coexist with an unglorified one, so a blessed angel with a bad one.
claims: Glorified bodies can co-locate with non-glorified ones (argument).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e959.summary: Second argument: angels are together with God, an immense spirit, so a fortiori one angel can be with another.
claims: Angels coexist with God (argument).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e966.summary: Third argument: body fills place more than spirit, and an angel can be with a body in the same place, so a fortiori with another angel.
claims: Angels can co-locate with bodies (argument).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e975.summary: Fourth argument: the soul is whole in every part of the body and an evil spirit sometimes enters a human body, so it is with the soul in the same place.
claims: Possessing spirits co-locate with the soul (argument).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e985.summary: Fifth argument: an angel does not fill place, so it cannot impede another; Mark 5's 'legion' of demons in one man implies many in one place.
claims: Angels do not fill place (argument).
A legion of demons inhabited one man.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e998.summary: Sixth argument: two distinct points can coincide, as when a perfect sphere touches a perfect plane; so indivisible angels can coincide.
claims: Two points can be together (argument).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e1014.summary: Seventh argument: many intelligible species are together in one intellect, so many intelligible angels in one place.
claims: Many species coexist in one intellect (argument).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e1023.summary: Sed contra: as body is to place circumscriptively, so angel definitively; two bodies cannot share a circumscribing place, so neither can two angels share a defining place.
claims: Definitive location excludes co-location as circumscription does.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e1036.summary: Second sed contra: Damascene proves there cannot be several gods because where one was the other would not be; likewise two angels cannot be in one place.
claims: Damascene's argument against many gods implies spiritual exclusion of place.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e1049.summary: Richard's solution: several angels cannot be in the same place by created power, because co-located things must penetrate each other, and no spirit can penetrate another by created power.
claims: Co-location requires mutual penetration.
No created spirit can penetrate another by created power.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e1070.summary: Reply to the first argument, first view: a glorified body coexists with an unglorified one only by uncreated power, which God's decree supplies at the soul's will; by such power a good spirit could also be with a bad one, but providence has not ordained that a good angel will it.
claims: Glorified bodies co-locate only by divine power at the soul's will.
Providence does not ordain good angels to will co-location with bad ones.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e1096.summary: Second view: a blessed angel could, by virtue of its beatitude, be with a bad angel if it willed, but God has ordained that it not will it, because it would be unfitting.
claims: Beatitude might give power to co-locate, but God ordains against it (alternative view).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e1107.summary: Reply to the second argument: angels are with God because God penetrates (illabitur) them, but one angel cannot penetrate another.
claims: Only God can penetrate created spirits.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e1114.summary: Reply to the third argument: an angel can be with a body because it can penetrate body, but not another angel.
claims: Angels can penetrate bodies but not other angels.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e1123.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: a possessing demon is not substantially in parts of the body perfected by the soul but in the humors or cavities (filled with air or vapor), which the soul does not inform; 'empty' is meant in the vulgar sense, since there is no void.
claims: Possessing demons occupy humors or cavities not informed by the soul.
There is no void.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e1145.summary: Reply to the fifth argument: the reason angels cannot co-locate is not that they fill place like bodies but that one cannot be penetrated by another through created power.
claims: Angelic exclusion derives from impenetrability, not repletion.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e1157.summary: Reply to the legion: the many demons were not in the same proper place but each in a distinct part of the body, since angelic space has no minimum and the continuum is endlessly divisible.
claims: Many demons can be in one body by occupying distinct parts.
The continuum is infinitely divisible.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e1173.summary: Reply to the points argument, first view: two points are together only negatively, with nothing between them, not as coinciding in a third point.
claims: Points are 'together' only by absence of an intermediary (one view).

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e1184.summary: Second view: two lines ending on a plane meet at one point (since between two points in a continuum there is always a line), so two points can coincide; but this does not transfer to angels, since a point has negative simplicity and an angel positive spiritual magnitude.
claims: Two points can coincide.
The point-angel analogy fails because their simplicities differ.

kzz7yh-a78920-d1e1210.summary: Reply to the intelligible species argument: species are in the intellect as accidents in a subject (Avicenna), whereas angels are in place as self-subsistent things.
claims: Intelligible species are accidents; angels are subsistent.

kzz7yh-a78920-Dd1e132.summary: Question 1 holds that an angel is not nowhere but is somewhere, definitively rather than circumscriptively. Richard rejects the view, condemned by Bishop Stephen at Paris, that angels are in place only by operation. His argument is that an angelic mover must be applied to the body it moves before it acts. The formal reason of an angel's location is its simultas (co-presence) with place, not circumscription, information or operation; its efficient causes are the angel's will and power or God's, and its final cause is the order of the universe. Authorities denying that spirits are in place mean circumscriptive place. Angelic location belongs to the accidental order of the universe, so God could change it, and it follows from the world as ordered, not from just any place.
claims: An angel is in place definitively, independent of operation.
The formal reason of angelic location is simultas with place.
The operation-only theory was rightly condemned.
Angelic location belongs to the accidental order of the universe.

kzz7yh-a78920-Dd1e540.summary: Question 2 holds that an angel is in extended corporeal space, whole in the whole and whole in each part, without commensuration or circumscription. The space it can occupy has a maximum but no minimum. Richard grounds this in a typology of four simplicities. A point has negative simplicity, separated body privative simplicity, and God positive simplicity of immensity. A created spirit has a positive but finite spiritual magnitude, a faint imitation of immensity, which lets an indivisible spirit be present to a divisible space. Opinion is reported on both sides of whether an angel can be in a point. Damascene's 'intelligibly' means non-circumscriptively.
claims: An angel is present to extended space whole in each part.
Created spirits have finite positive spiritual magnitude.
Angelic space has a maximum but no minimum.

kzz7yh-a78920-Dd1e748.summary: Question 3 denies that an angel can be in several places at once by any created power. Definitive location means being defined by one place, and the space an angel occupies has a maximum, which multilocation would abolish; the contradiction is nearly self-evident. Hugh's claim concerns only supernatural divine power, and Richard of St Victor's one wisdom in many refers to uncreated wisdom. The bilocation of Ambrose and the wandering 'phantasticum' are explained as miracle or as apparitions of spirits in human likeness. Parts of different bodies within the angel's maximum space count as one place.
claims: An angel cannot be in several places by created power.
Reported bilocations are miracles or angelic or demonic apparitions.

kzz7yh-a78920-Dd1e942.summary: Question 4 denies that several angels can occupy the same proper place by created power. Co-location requires mutual penetration, and no created spirit can penetrate another; only God 'illabitur' spirits, and angels can penetrate bodies but not one another. Glorified bodies co-locate only by divine power, and providence does not ordain good angels to will co-location with bad. Possessing demons occupy humors or cavities, not the soul's place, and a legion occupies distinct parts of an infinitely divisible body. The analogies from coinciding points and from intelligible species fail because of differences in simplicity and subsistence.
claims: Two angels cannot be in one place by created power.
The obstacle is impenetrability, not repletion of place.
Only God penetrates created spirits.

kzz7yh-a78920.summary: Article 2 of I d.37 develops Richard's theory of angelic location in four questions. An angel is not nowhere but is in place definitively, independent of operation. Against the condemned operation-only view, a mover must be present before it acts, and the formal reason of location is the angel's simultas with place. It is present in extended space, whole in the whole and in each part, thanks to its positive but finite spiritual magnitude, set within a typology of four simplicities; that space has a maximum but no minimum. It cannot be in several places at once by created power, and stories of bilocation are explained as miracles or apparitions. Two angels cannot share one place, because no created spirit can penetrate another.
claims: Angels are in place definitively by simultas, not by operation alone.
Angels have finite positive spiritual magnitude, giving them a maximal space with no minimum.
Angels cannot be multilocated or co-located by created power.
